s3-l001-equivalence-principle-free-fall.prompt: What does an Eötvös-type torsion-balance experiment actually test?
options: The gravitational force between two masses falls off as exactly $1/r^2$ down to laboratory distances, with no deviation.
Whether a beam of light is deflected by the Earth's gravitational field by the angle predicted for a massive particle.
Different materials accelerate identically: $m_{\rm grav}/m_{\rm inertial}$ is the same for all bodies.
That Newton's constant $G$ was the same at all epochs in the history of the universe, with no drift in time.
s3-l001-equivalence-principle-free-fall.explanation: The balance hangs two different materials; Earth's gravity and the inertial (centrifugal) effect of Earth's rotation point in slightly different directions, so any composition dependence of $m_{\rm grav}/m_{\rm inertial}$ would twist the beam. Null results at the $10^{-13}$ level or better are the weak equivalence principle.

s3-l001-equivalence-principle-free-fall.prompt: Free fall is universal, so a freely falling lab can cancel gravity locally. Why does this not let us remove gravity everywhere with one clever choice of frame?
options: Inertial and gravitational mass differ slightly for large bodies, so a large lab cannot be in free fall at all.
Freely falling frames always rotate relative to the distant stars, so gravity returns as a Coriolis-type force.
Gravity acts instantaneously over any distance, so no motion of the lab could ever cancel it, even locally.
The field varies from place to place, so nearby free-falling particles accelerate relative to each other.
s3-l001-equivalence-principle-free-fall.explanation: Cancelling gravity at a point uses the fact that every body falls the same way there. Away from that point the gravitational field has a different direction and strength, so nearby free-falling bodies drift apart or together. These tidal accelerations are the physical signature of curvature.

s3-l001-equivalence-principle-free-fall.prompt: In your own words, explain why the universality of free fall (every body falls the same way regardless of mass or composition) suggests that gravity is a property of spacetime geometry rather than an ordinary force.
s3-l001-equivalence-principle-free-fall.rubric: Full credit: (1) universality means the motion of a freely falling body depends only on position and velocity, not on any property of the body (an ordinary force like the electric one depends on charge-to-mass ratio); (2) so the motion can be attributed to the background arena, spacetime, with free fall being the 'straightest' path (geodesic); (3) mentions that the local-inertial-frame idea works only locally and the leftover tidal effects are the curvature.
s3-l001-equivalence-principle-free-fall.modelAnswer: If gravity were a force with its own coupling, different bodies would respond differently, as charged particles do with different charge-to-mass ratios. Because every body, whatever its mass or composition, follows the same trajectory from the same initial conditions, it is more economical to say they all follow the natural straight lines (geodesics) of the spacetime itself. Locally you can always go into a freely falling frame where gravity disappears, and what cannot be removed, the tidal variation from place to place, is the curvature of spacetime.

s3-l002-gravitational-redshift-gps-clock.prompt: A photon of frequency $f$ is emitted upward from the ground and received at the top of a tower of height $h$ on Earth. Which description is correct?
options: Its frequency is lower by $\Delta f/f = gh/c^2$; its local speed stays $c$, but it loses energy climbing.
Its speed drops to $c - gh/c$ at the top of the tower, while its frequency stays the same as at emission.
Its frequency is higher by $gh/c^2$, since the photon is attracted by the Earth and gains energy as it travels.
Nothing changes: a massless photon has no gravitational mass, so it does not couple to gravity at all.
s3-l002-gravitational-redshift-gps-clock.explanation: In the accelerating-elevator picture the receiver at the top is moving away from where the light was emitted by the time it arrives, so it is Doppler-redshifted by $g h/c^2$. By the equivalence principle the same holds in a gravitational field, and the effect is in agreement with the Pound-Rebka experiment.

s3-l002-gravitational-redshift-gps-clock.prompt: A GPS satellite orbits at $r = 26{,}560$ km from Earth's centre; a ground clock sits at $R = 6371$ km. Use only the gravitational-potential part of the weak-field time dilation, $\Delta\tau/\tau = \Delta\Phi/c^2$ with $\Phi=-GM/r$ ($GM_\oplus = 3.986\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^3/s^2}$). By how many microseconds per day does the satellite clock run faster than the ground clock from this effect alone? (Give the answer in $\mu$s/day.)
s3-l002-gravitational-redshift-gps-clock.explanation: $\Delta\tau/\tau = (GM/c^2)(1/R - 1/r) \approx 5.29e-10$, which over 86,400 s is about 45.7 $\mu$s. Orbital speed contributes about $-7\ \mu$s/day, so the net is roughly $+38\ \mu$s/day, which must be corrected for or positions drift by about 10 km per day.

s3-l002-gravitational-redshift-gps-clock.prompt: A GPS satellite clock is compared with a clock on the ground. Explain in your own words why gravity makes the orbiting clock tick faster, why its speed makes it tick slower, and why the net difference must be corrected.
s3-l002-gravitational-redshift-gps-clock.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) higher in the potential (less negative $\Phi$) means a faster clock, about +45 us/day for GPS; (2) a moving clock runs slow by about $v^2/2c^2$, about -7 us/day; (3) the net is about +38 us/day, which would grow into position errors of order 10 km per day (38 us times c) if it were not corrected.
s3-l002-gravitational-redshift-gps-clock.modelAnswer: Clocks higher in a gravitational potential run faster ($\Delta\tau/\tau=\Delta\Phi/c^2$), giving about +45 us/day for a GPS satellite, while its orbital speed slows it by about 7 us/day. The net +38 us/day, multiplied by $c$, would produce kilometre-scale position errors within a day, so the clocks are deliberately adjusted.

s3-l003-interval-boosts-time-dilation.prompt: In one inertial frame, two events along the $x$-axis are separated by $\Delta t = 5$ s and $\Delta x = 3$ light-seconds. They are timelike-separated. How much proper time (in seconds) elapses between them on a clock that is present at both events?
s3-l003-interval-boosts-time-dilation.explanation: $\Delta s^2 = -c^2\Delta t^2 + \Delta x^2 = -(25-9)$ in light-second units, so $c\,\Delta\tau = \sqrt{16} = 4$ s. A frame moving at $v = 3c/5$ sees both events at the same place, where the elapsed time is 4 s.

s3-l003-interval-boosts-time-dilation.prompt: Cosmic-ray muons (rest lifetime about 2.2 $\mu$s) created high in the atmosphere reach the ground even though $c \times 2.2\ \mu\mathrm{s} \approx 660$ m. How do the Earth frame and the muon frame each explain this, and why don't they disagree?
options: Earth frame: the muon's lifetime is truly lengthened. Muon frame: the atmosphere keeps its full thickness, so the muon must decay; the frames disagree.
Earth frame: the muon's clock runs slow. Muon frame: the atmosphere is length-contracted. Both agree it reaches the ground.
In both frames the muon moves at nearly $c$, so the atmosphere is thin in both and no correction to the lifetime is needed.
The muon exceeds $c$ in the Earth frame, which lets it cover the distance before it can decay in its own frame.
s3-l003-interval-boosts-time-dilation.explanation: Time dilation and length contraction are two descriptions of the same boost. What is frame-independent is the spacetime interval between the 'created' and 'arrives at ground' events, and whether the muon survives is an invariant fact about those events.

s3-l003-interval-boosts-time-dilation.prompt: Time dilation and length contraction are both frame-dependent. Explain in your own words why the spacetime interval is nonetheless the 'real' invariant quantity, and how the two effects are consistent with it.
s3-l003-interval-boosts-time-dilation.rubric: Full credit: (1) states the interval $-c^2\Delta t^2+\Delta x^2$ takes the same value in all inertial frames (a boost rotates $(ct,x)$ the way a spatial rotation rotates $(x,y)$); (2) time dilation/length contraction arise from projecting a fixed 4D separation onto different time and space axes; (3) a clock's proper time is the invariant quantity; no contradiction since different frames split the interval into 'time' and 'space' parts differently.
s3-l003-interval-boosts-time-dilation.modelAnswer: A boost mixes time and space the way a rotation mixes $x$ and $y$, and the quantity $-c^2\Delta t^2 + \Delta x^2$ is the analogue of the invariant length. Different observers slice the same four-dimensional separation into different time and space parts, so the time between events (time dilation) and the length of a moving rod (length contraction) differ between frames. The proper time along a worldline, the interval itself, is the thing all observers agree on.

s3-l004-four-vectors-proper-time-twins.prompt: With signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and $p^\mu = (E/c,\ \mathbf p)$, evaluating $p^\mu p_\mu$ gives the same number in every inertial frame. What is it, and what does that tell you?
options: $+E^2/c^2 + |\mathbf p|^2$: energy and momentum add in quadrature, so the 'size' of the four-momentum grows with speed.
$-E^2/c^2 + |\mathbf p|^2 = -m^2c^2$: a fixed Minkowski length set by the rest mass, so $E^2 = p^2c^2 + m^2c^4$ in every frame.
$-E^2/c^2 - |\mathbf p|^2$: lowering the index flips every component's sign, so the result is always negative and frame dependent.
$+m^2c^2$: the squared magnitude of any four-vector is positive, and a sign flip appears only when a particle is off shell.
s3-l004-four-vectors-proper-time-twins.explanation: Lowering an index with $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ flips the sign of the time component only (in this signature). The contraction is a Lorentz scalar, so it can be evaluated in the rest frame where it equals $-m^2c^2$; for a photon it is zero (null four-momentum).

s3-l004-four-vectors-proper-time-twins.prompt: One twin stays on an inertial worldline between two events; the other travels out and back, accelerating at the turnaround. Which statement is correct?
options: The traveller ages more, because a longer path accumulates more proper time, just as for distances in Euclidean geometry.
Neither ages less: each twin sees the other's clock run slow, so the situation is completely symmetric.
The traveller ages less only because of the turnaround; the cruising legs themselves produce no time dilation at all.
The traveller ages less: the inertial straight worldline has the longest proper time of all timelike paths.
s3-l004-four-vectors-proper-time-twins.explanation: Proper time is the 'length' of a worldline in a Lorentzian geometry, where the straight line maximises it. The situation is not symmetric because only the stay-at-home twin is inertial between the two events; the traveller's worldline changes frames.

s3-l004-four-vectors-proper-time-twins.prompt: Using signature $(-,+,+,+)$, evaluate $x^\mu x_\mu=\eta_{\mu\nu}x^\mu x^\nu$ for an event with $(ct,x,y,z)=(5,3,0,0)$ light-seconds. Give the answer in (light-seconds)$^2$.
s3-l004-four-vectors-proper-time-twins.explanation: $x^\mu x_\mu=-(ct)^2+x^2=-25+9=-16$. The negative sign means the event is timelike separated from the origin.

s3-l004-four-vectors-proper-time-twins.prompt: Explain in your own words why $p^\mu p_\mu=-m^2c^2$ has the same value in every inertial frame, and what it says about the energy of a particle at rest and of a photon.
s3-l004-four-vectors-proper-time-twins.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $p^\mu$ is a four-vector and contracting it with $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ gives an invariant, so evaluate it in the rest frame where $p^\mu=(mc,\mathbf 0)$ to get $-m^2c^2$; (2) in any frame this reads $E^2=p^2c^2+m^2c^4$, so $E=mc^2$ at rest; (3) for a photon $m=0$, so $E=pc$ and its four-momentum is null.
s3-l004-four-vectors-proper-time-twins.modelAnswer: The contraction of a four-vector with itself is invariant, and in the rest frame it equals $-m^2c^2$, so in every frame $E^2=p^2c^2+m^2c^4$. At rest this gives $E=mc^2$; for a photon, with $m=0$, it gives $E=pc$ and a null four-momentum.

s3-l005-metric-line-element-coordinates.prompt: On a sphere of radius $R$ with $ds^2 = R^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\, d\phi^2)$, draw the circle of all points at surface distance $r = \pi R/2$ from the north pole (that is, the equator). What is the ratio (circumference)/(radius), with both measured along the surface? (A flat plane would give $2\pi \approx 6.28$.)
s3-l005-metric-line-element-coordinates.explanation: The circumference is $\oint R\sin\theta\,d\phi = 2\pi R\sin(\pi/2) = 2\pi R$ and the radius (measured along the surface) is $\pi R/2$, so the ratio is $4$. Being smaller than $2\pi$ is an intrinsic signal of positive curvature, with no reference to any embedding in 3D.

s3-l005-metric-line-element-coordinates.prompt: The metric $ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2\,d\theta^2$ has a coefficient $r^2$ that varies with position. Is this space curved?
options: No. It is the flat plane in polar coordinates ($x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$); curvature is not read off the coefficients.
Yes. A coefficient that varies with position means distances are stretched differently at different $r$, which is what curvature is.
Yes, but only near $r=0$, where the coordinates break down and triangle angle sums deviate from $180^\circ$.
No, but only because $r^2$ grows with $r$; a coefficient that shrank with $r$ would signal curvature.
s3-l005-metric-line-element-coordinates.explanation: Coordinate-dependent features such as position-dependent metric components can be artifacts of the labels. The invariant tests are measurable things, like whether the angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ$ or whether circumference/radius is $2\pi$; both pass here.

s3-l005-metric-line-element-coordinates.prompt: On a sphere of radius $R=2$ m with $dA=R^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi$, find the area of the northern hemisphere $0\le\theta\le\pi/2$. Give the answer in m$^2$.
In your own words: what does a line element $ds^2=g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu$ let you compute, and why do coordinate values such as $\theta$ or $r$ carry no physical meaning without it?
s3-l005-metric-line-element-coordinates.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the metric converts coordinate differences into physical lengths and times, e.g. the length of a curve is $\int\sqrt{g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu}\,d\lambda$; (2) coordinates are just labels, and one geometry has many coordinate descriptions (Cartesian versus polar), so only invariants like lengths and areas are physical; (3) an example such as $d\phi=1$ rad being a different physical length at different latitudes.
s3-l005-metric-line-element-coordinates.modelAnswer: The metric turns coordinate differences into physical distances and proper times, so lengths, areas and volumes follow from integrating $ds$. Coordinates are only labels: on a sphere the same $d\phi$ corresponds to a physical length $R\sin\theta\,d\phi$ that depends on latitude, so without the metric the numbers mean nothing.

s3-l006-local-inertial-frames-light-cone.prompt: In the metric $ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + 4\,dx^2$ (one space dimension), light has coordinate speed $dx/dt = c/2$. What does this mean?
options: Light genuinely travels at half speed in this region, just as it would in a medium with refractive index 2.
The metric must be wrong, because the speed of light has to equal $c$ in every coordinate system.
Nothing physical: $x$ is just a label with proper length $2\,dx$, so the locally measured speed of light is still $c$.
Light and clocks are both slowed by the same factor, so the proper speed of light is $c$ only far from the origin.
s3-l006-local-inertial-frames-light-cone.explanation: Null directions satisfy $ds^2 = 0$: $c\,dt = 2\,dx$. Coordinate speeds depend on the labelling; what is invariant is the light cone and the speed measured with proper lengths and proper times, which is always $c$.

Why can one always choose coordinates in which $g_{\mu
u} = \eta_{\mu
u}$ and $\partial_\lambda g_{\mu
u} = 0$ at a given point, but not in a neighbourhood?
options: Curvature vanishes at every individual point, even though it can be nonzero over extended regions of space.
Every metric is flat in suitable coordinates, so a neighbourhood version also exists; it is just harder to construct.
Gravity is a force that can be switched off at a point by an accelerating frame, but not at neighbouring points.
Coordinates can cancel the metric's deviation from $\eta$ and its first derivatives at a point, not the second.
s3-l006-local-inertial-frames-light-cone.explanation: Counting the free coordinate functions shows that they can set $g$ and $\partial g$ to the flat values at a point. The second derivatives of the metric contain independent information (Riemann curvature) that no coordinate change can eliminate. This is the mathematical form of 'free fall removes gravity only locally'.

s3-l006-local-inertial-frames-light-cone.prompt: You are an inhabitant of a two-dimensional surface and cannot step 'off' it. Describe two measurements you could make to decide whether your surface is intrinsically curved, and explain what each would show on a sphere.
s3-l006-local-inertial-frames-light-cone.rubric: Full credit: names two valid intrinsic tests, e.g. (a) circumference vs. radius of circles ($C<2\pi r$ on a sphere), (b) angle sum of a triangle (>180° on a sphere), (c) area of a disc vs $\pi r^2$, (d) parallel-transport/triangle geodesics converging; states sphere results correctly; makes clear these do not need an embedding space.
s3-l006-local-inertial-frames-light-cone.modelAnswer: Draw a circle by marking all points at the same surface distance $r$ from a centre and measure its circumference: in flat space $C = 2\pi r$, but on a sphere $C = 2\pi R\sin(r/R) < 2\pi r$. Or measure the interior angles of a triangle made of geodesic segments: they sum to $180^\circ$ in flat space and to more than $180^\circ$ on a sphere (the excess is the area divided by $R^2$). Both use only distances and angles within the surface, so no embedding is needed.

s3-l007-geodesic-equation-christoffel-sy.prompt: In flat 2D space with polar coordinates, a free particle moving in a straight line has $d^2r/ds^2 \ne 0$ (the Christoffel symbol $\Gamma^r{}_{\theta\theta} = -r$ enters). What does this show?
options: A real force pulls the particle off a straight path; straight lines have constant $r$ only in Cartesian coordinates.
The $\Gamma$ terms reflect changing basis vectors, not a force or curvature; flat space can have nonzero $\Gamma$.
The straight line is not a geodesic in polar coordinates, because geodesics must have $d^2x^\mu/ds^2=0$ in every system.
Nonzero Christoffel symbols prove the space is curved, so the plane in polar coordinates is intrinsically curved at $r\neq0$.
s3-l007-geodesic-equation-christoffel-sy.explanation: The geodesic equation is $\ddot x^\mu + \Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}\dot x^\alpha\dot x^\beta = 0$. In polar coordinates the term $-r\dot\theta^2$ is the 'centrifugal' coordinate effect, which compensates the change of basis. $\Gamma$ is not a tensor and can be nonzero even in flat space.

s3-l007-geodesic-equation-christoffel-sy.prompt: For the 2-sphere $ds^2=R^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)$ the Euler-Lagrange equation for $\theta$ reads $\ddot\theta-\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\phi^2=0$, so $\Gamma^\theta{}_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$. Evaluate $\Gamma^\theta{}_{\phi\phi}$ at $\theta=\pi/3$ (dimensionless).
Explain in your own words why extremizing the proper time along a path leads to the geodesic equation, and what the Christoffel-symbol term represents.
s3-l007-geodesic-equation-christoffel-sy.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) proper time is $\tau=\int\sqrt{-g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu}\,d\lambda/c$ and the Euler-Lagrange equations of this functional give a second-order equation for $x^\mu(\tau)$; (2) the result $\ddot x^\mu+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}\dot x^\alpha\dot x^\beta=0$ describes the 'straightest' path; (3) the $\Gamma$ terms encode how the coordinate basis changes from point to point (nonzero even in flat space in curvilinear coordinates) and play the role of the inertial or gravitational acceleration in the chosen coordinates.
s3-l007-geodesic-equation-christoffel-sy.modelAnswer: The proper time functional has a stationary path whose Euler-Lagrange equations are $\ddot x^\mu+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}\dot x^\alpha\dot x^\beta=0$: the straightest possible path. The $\Gamma$ terms measure how the coordinate basis varies from place to place, which is why they can appear even in flat space with curved coordinates and act like a coordinate-dependent acceleration.

s3-l008-conserved-quantities-newtonian-l.prompt: A metric has components that do not depend on the coordinate $\phi$. What follows for geodesic motion?
options: The angular velocity $d\phi/d\tau$ is constant along every geodesic, whatever the other coordinates do.
Every geodesic stays at constant $r$ or moves on a circle of constant radius around the origin of $\phi$.
The covariant component $p_\phi = m\,g_{\phi\mu}\,dx^\mu/d\tau$ is conserved along every geodesic.
All Christoffel symbols carrying a $\phi$ index vanish, so $\phi$ behaves like a Cartesian coordinate.
s3-l008-conserved-quantities-newtonian-l.explanation: The Euler-Lagrange equation for $\phi$ reads $\frac{d}{d\tau}\!\left(\partial L/\partial\dot\phi\right) = \partial L/\partial\phi = 0$. Symmetry gives a conserved quantity: independence of $t$ gives energy, of $\phi$ gives angular momentum. The conserved thing is $p_\phi$, not $\dot\phi$.

s3-l008-conserved-quantities-newtonian-l.prompt: For a slowly moving particle in a weak field, $g_{00} = -(1 + 2\Phi/c^2)$ reproduces Newtonian gravity, $\ddot{\mathbf x} = -\nabla\Phi$. Why does only $g_{00}$ matter at this order?
options: Since $dx^0/d\tau\approx c$ dominates, the geodesic equation reduces to $\ddot x^i\approx\tfrac12c^2\partial_ig_{00}$.
The spatial components $g_{ij}$ are exactly flat in any gravitational field, so only the time component can change.
Time dilation is the only relativistic effect at this order, and the geometry of space plays no role in any experiment.
All the Christoffel symbols are equal at this order, so any component of the metric would give the same result.
s3-l008-conserved-quantities-newtonian-l.explanation: For $v \ll c$, every term with a spatial velocity is suppressed by $v/c$. The surviving term is $\Gamma^i{}_{00}$, which involves $\partial_i g_{00}$. Spatial curvature $g_{ij}$ matters only for fast particles (this is why light bends twice the Newtonian amount).

s3-l008-conserved-quantities-newtonian-l.prompt: At Earth's surface, the time-time metric component differs from its flat-space value by $|g_{00} + 1| = 2GM/(Rc^2)$. Using $GM_\oplus = 3.986\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^3/s^2}$, $R = 6.371\times10^6$ m and $c = 2.998\times10^8$ m/s, give this number in units of $10^{-9}$.
s3-l008-conserved-quantities-newtonian-l.explanation: $2GM/(Rc^2) = 1.392e-09$, about one part in a billion: gravity on Earth is an extremely weak perturbation of flat spacetime, which is why Newtonian physics works so well.

s3-l008-conserved-quantities-newtonian-l.prompt: Explain why light rays cannot be described by extremizing proper time, and how the geodesic description is modified for light.
s3-l008-conserved-quantities-newtonian-l.rubric:
Full credit: (1) for light $ds^2 = 0$, so proper time along the path is zero and cannot be used as parameter or as the quantity to extremize; (2) null geodesics are obtained with an affine parameter $\lambda$ (e.g. extremizing $\int g_{\mu
u}\dot x^\mu \dot x^
u d\lambda$) with the constraint $g_{\mu
u}\dot x^\mu\dot x^
u = 0$; (3) same geodesic equation, conserved quantities carry over, or light as limit of massless particle.
s3-l008-conserved-quantities-newtonian-l.modelAnswer: A photon's worldline is null, $ds^2 = 0$, so the proper time along it is zero and the 'longest proper time' principle is empty. Instead one uses an affine parameter $\lambda$ along the path, with the same geodesic equation $\ddot x^\mu + \Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}\dot x^\alpha \dot x^\beta = 0$, and imposes the null condition $g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu \dot x^\nu = 0$ as a constraint. Conserved quantities from symmetries still apply.

s3-l009-schwarzschild-metric-redshift.prompt: Compute the Schwarzschild radius $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ of the Earth ($GM_\oplus = 3.986\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^3/s^2}$). Give the answer in millimetres.
s3-l009-schwarzschild-metric-redshift.explanation: $r_s = 2GM/c^2 = 8.87$ mm. Squeezing the entire Earth into a marble-sized sphere would be needed to form a black hole; the Sun's value is about 2.95 km.

s3-l009-schwarzschild-metric-redshift.prompt: In the Schwarzschild metric, what does the coordinate $r$ mean physically?
options: The areal radius: a sphere at coordinate $r$ has area $4\pi r^2$; radial proper distances exceed $\Delta r$.
The proper distance from the centre to the point, found by laying rulers end to end along a radial line.
The distance a faraway observer infers from radar echoes: half the round-trip light time multiplied by $c$.
The radial distance only for light rays; for massive observers $r$ has no geometric meaning whatsoever.
s3-l009-schwarzschild-metric-redshift.explanation: The angular part $r^2 d\Omega^2$ guarantees that circumferences are $2\pi r$, but the radial term $dr^2/(1-r_s/r)$ means a radial ruler stretches. Spacetime is curved, so there is no flat 'distance to the centre' in the Euclidean sense.
