u} = \eta_{\mu
u} + h_{\mu
u}$, looks a lot like electromagnetism with retarded potentials. List one important similarity and one important difference between the two radiation problems.
s3-l037-linearized-einstein-equation-ret.rubric: Full credit: similarity: wave equation with source in Lorenz/harmonic gauge solved by retarded Green's function; waves at $c$; $1/r$ radiation field; or energy flux. Difference: gravity's source is a rank-2 tensor / spin-2 so quadrupole is leading (dipole forbidden by momentum conservation), whereas EM has dipole radiation from vector source; or gravity gravitates (nonlinear), or only one sign of charge.
s3-l037-linearized-einstein-equation-ret.modelAnswer: Both are wave equations for a potential ($A_\mu$ or $\bar h_{\mu\nu}$) sourced by a conserved current ($J_\mu$ or $T_{\mu\nu}$), in Lorenz gauge, solved by retarded solutions; the radiation travels at $c$ and falls off as $1/r$. The difference is that the gravitational source is a tensor with only one sign of charge, so conservation of momentum kills the dipole term and the lowest radiation is quadrupolar (spin 2), and that the full theory is nonlinear because gravity itself carries energy.

s3-l037-linearized-einstein-equation-ret.prompt: What does the Lorenz (harmonic) gauge condition $\partial_\mu\bar h^{\mu\nu}=0$ accomplish in linearized gravity?
options: It turns the linearized field equations into the wave equations $\Box\bar h_{\mu\nu}=-16\pi GT_{\mu\nu}/c^4$.
It sets $h_{\mu\nu}=0$ outside the source, so there are no waves in vacuum.
It removes the physical polarizations of the gravitational wave from the solution.
It makes the linearized equations exact for arbitrarily strong gravitational fields.
s3-l037-linearized-einstein-equation-ret.explanation: The gauge condition kills the extra derivative terms in the linearized Einstein tensor, leaving a wave equation for each component of $\bar h_{\mu\nu}$ with source $T_{\mu\nu}$, ready for the retarded Green's function.

s3-l038-quadrupole-formula-no-dipole-rad.prompt: Why does gravity have no monopole or dipole radiation, so the leading gravitational radiation is quadrupolar?
options: Spherically symmetric sources do not exist in nature, so monopole radiation is impossible.
They exist but are too weak compared with the quadrupole for any known astrophysical source.
Gravitational waves are transverse, and a transverse wave cannot be produced by a dipole.
Conservation of energy and momentum forbids both monopole and dipole radiation.
s3-l038-quadrupole-formula-no-dipole-rad.explanation: In electromagnetism a dipole is allowed because charges come in both signs, and the dipole moment can change even if total charge is conserved. For mass, $\ddot{\mathbf d} \propto \dot{\mathbf P} = 0$ by momentum conservation. Thus the first allowed radiation is from the mass quadrupole: $h\sim G\ddot Q/(c^4 r)$.

s3-l038-quadrupole-formula-no-dipole-rad.prompt: Which of these systems radiates gravitational waves in the quadrupole approximation?
options: A perfectly spherical star rotating uniformly about an axis through its centre at constant angular velocity.
A thin rod tumbling end over end: its quadrupole changes in time, radiating at twice the rotation frequency.
A spherical star pulsating radially, expanding and contracting while staying exactly spherical.
A perfectly axisymmetric disk spinning at constant angular velocity about its own symmetry axis.
s3-l038-quadrupole-formula-no-dipole-rad.explanation: The radiation requires $\dddot Q_{ij}\neq 0$. Rotation about a symmetry axis or radial pulsations leave the mass quadrupole constant or zero. The rod's quadrupole returns to itself after half a turn, hence frequency $2f_{\rm rot}$. A circular binary radiates the same way.

s3-l038-quadrupole-formula-no-dipole-rad.prompt: Explain in words what the quadrupole formula says about how the wave amplitude depends on the source and on the distance $r$, and why a source must be both asymmetric and time-dependent to radiate.
s3-l038-quadrupole-formula-no-dipole-rad.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $h_{ij}\propto(2G/c^4r)\,\ddot Q_{ij}$ evaluated at the retarded time $t-r/c$; (2) the amplitude falls as $1/r$; (3) a static or spherically symmetric distribution has $\ddot Q_{ij}=0$ and does not radiate, while a rotating dumbbell or binary radiates at twice its rotation frequency.
s3-l038-quadrupole-formula-no-dipole-rad.modelAnswer: The amplitude is $h_{ij}=(2G/c^4r)\ddot Q_{ij}(t-r/c)$: it is set by the second time derivative of the mass quadrupole at the retarded time and falls as $1/r$. A static or spherical mass distribution has no changing quadrupole and so does not radiate, whereas a rotating dumbbell or a binary does.

s3-l039-binary-inspiral-orbital-decay-co.prompt: Two $1.4\,M_\odot$ neutron stars orbit each other on a circular orbit of separation $a = 1.95\times10^9$ m (similar to the Hulse-Taylor pulsar). Use the quadrupole formula's result $t_{\rm coal} = \dfrac{5}{256}\dfrac{c^5 a^4}{G^3 m_1 m_2 (m_1+m_2)}$ to estimate the time to merger, in years. ($G=6.674\times10^{-11}$, $M_\odot = 1.989\times10^{30}$ kg.)
s3-l039-binary-inspiral-orbital-decay-co.explanation: $t_{\rm coal} = 5.33e+16$ s $\approx 1.69e+09$ yr, about 1.7 billion years for a circular orbit (the real PSR B1913+16 is eccentric, $e\approx0.62$, which speeds the merger up to about 300 Myr). Since $t\propto a^4$, halving the separation shortens the time by a factor of 16.

s3-l039-binary-inspiral-orbital-decay-co.prompt: The Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar has an orbital period of 7.75 hours. A circular binary radiates gravitational waves at twice the orbital frequency. What is the gravitational-wave frequency, in units of $10^{-5}$ Hz?
s3-l039-binary-inspiral-orbital-decay-co.explanation: $f_{\rm GW}=2/P=2/(7.75\times3600\ \mathrm{s})\approx7.17\times10^{-5}$ Hz, far below LIGO's band; it will sweep upward only in the last minutes before merger.

s3-l039-binary-inspiral-orbital-decay-co.prompt: As a circular binary inspirals by emitting gravitational waves, what happens to its orbital period and to the power it radiates?
options: The period grows because the waves carry away angular momentum, and the radiated power falls.
Both stay constant until the two stars finally touch, at which point the radiation starts.
The period shrinks and the power grows as $a^{-5}$, so the decay accelerates toward merger.
The period shrinks, but the radiated power falls because the stars move more slowly.
s3-l039-binary-inspiral-orbital-decay-co.explanation: Energy loss lowers the separation $a$, which raises the orbital frequency; the power scales as $a^{-5}$, so the closer the stars get, the faster they lose energy and the faster the orbit shrinks.

s3-l039-binary-inspiral-orbital-decay-co.prompt: Explain why the coalescence time scales as $a^4$, and what this implies about how a binary spends its life before it merges.
s3-l039-binary-inspiral-orbital-decay-co.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) radiated power scales as $a^{-5}$ while the orbital energy scales as $1/a$, so $da/dt\propto a^{-3}$ and integrating gives $t\propto a^4$; (2) a wide binary shrinks very slowly, so most of its life is spent in a nearly constant orbit; (3) the decay runs away at the end, and the final stages (the chirp seen by LIGO) take only seconds to minutes.
s3-l039-binary-inspiral-orbital-decay-co.modelAnswer: Since power $\propto a^{-5}$ and energy $\propto1/a$, we get $da/dt\propto a^{-3}$ and $t_{\rm coal}\propto a^4$. A wide binary therefore changes very slowly for most of its life, but the shrinking runs away at the end, so the last inspiral and merger are over in seconds to minutes.

s3-l040-frw-metric-friedmann-equations.prompt: In the FRW picture, distant galaxies recede from us. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Galaxies were flung outward from a central point and move through a fixed background space at speeds set by the initial explosion.
Space expands inside every bound system, atoms and galaxies included, but our rulers expand too, so we cannot measure it.
Galaxies move through space, and those receding faster than $c$ have broken special relativity locally.
Comoving galaxies keep fixed coordinates while $a(t)$ grows: the space between them stretches.
s3-l040-frw-metric-friedmann-equations.explanation: The metric $ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + a(t)^2[\ldots]$ tells you proper distance between comoving points is $a(t)\chi$. Recession speed $v = H d$ can exceed $c$ at large distance without violating relativity, which only restricts local motion relative to the Hubble flow.

s3-l040-frw-metric-friedmann-equations.prompt: The acceleration equation is $\ddot a/a = -\tfrac{4\pi G}{3}(\rho + 3p/c^2) + \Lambda c^2/3$. What is needed for the expansion to accelerate?
options: A component with sufficiently negative pressure, $p<-\rho c^2/3$, such as a cosmological constant.
A very large positive pressure, which pushes the universe outward faster than gravity pulls it in.
A negative mass density, since any positive density always decelerates the expansion.
A matter density above the critical density, whose extra gravity speeds the expansion up.
s3-l040-frw-metric-friedmann-equations.explanation: Positive pressure adds to deceleration in GR because it contributes to the gravitating source. Negative pressure that is more negative than $-\rho c^2/3$ makes $\rho + 3p/c^2<0$ and yields repulsion. This is what dark energy is inferred to do.

s3-l040-frw-metric-friedmann-equations.prompt: The Newtonian derivation of the Friedmann equation uses a shell of dust in a gravitating sphere. State two things that the GR derivation adds, and explain the physical meaning of the curvature constant $k$.
s3-l040-frw-metric-friedmann-equations.rubric: Full credit: (1) GR gives meaning to $k$: the spatial curvature of the universe (closed $k=+1$, flat $0$, open $-1$), whereas in Newton it is just an energy (integration) constant; (2) pressure is a source of gravity ($\rho+3p/c^2$), also Lambda and radiation fall naturally into the formalism; (3) it applies to the whole of space including radiation and beyond the horizon, consistent with relativity.
s3-l040-frw-metric-friedmann-equations.modelAnswer: In the Newtonian derivation the term $-kc^2/a^2$ is just the total energy of a test shell. In GR it is the curvature of space itself: $k=+1$ is a closed universe like a 3-sphere, $k=0$ is flat, and $k=-1$ is open (negatively curved), with flatness corresponding to the critical density. GR also tells us that pressure gravitates (the $\rho + 3p/c^2$ combination), which lets radiation and dark energy be included consistently.

s3-l041-scale-factor-solutions-matter-ra.prompt: In a flat universe dominated by matter, $a\propto t^{2/3}$ and the age is $t_0 = 2/(3H_0)$. For $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc (1 Mpc $= 3.086\times10^{22}$ m), find $t_0$ in billions of years.
s3-l041-scale-factor-solutions-matter-ra.explanation: $H_0 = 2.269e-18\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, so $t_0 = 2/(3H_0) = 9.31$ Gyr. This is shorter than the age of the oldest stars and the ΛCDM value ($\approx 13.8$ Gyr), one of the early arguments for a cosmological constant.

s3-l041-scale-factor-solutions-matter-ra.prompt: Why did radiation dominate the early universe, while matter dominates later and (today) dark energy takes over?
options: Radiation is gradually converted into matter as the universe cools, and matter into dark energy as structures form.
All three components dilute the same way with volume, so their ratios are fixed by the initial conditions.
Matter dilutes as $a^{-3}$, radiation as $a^{-4}$, and Lambda not at all, so the slowest-diluting wins late.
Radiation density falls as $a^{-2}$ because photons spread over areas, matter as $a^{-3}$, and Lambda as $a^{-4}$.
s3-l041-scale-factor-solutions-matter-ra.explanation: The Friedmann equation then gives $a\propto t^{1/2}$ for radiation, $t^{2/3}$ for matter, and $e^{Ht}$ for Lambda. The universe passes through these epochs in that order.

s3-l041-scale-factor-solutions-matter-ra.prompt: In a flat universe dominated by radiation, how does the scale factor grow compared with a matter-dominated one?
options: As $a\propto t^{1/2}$, more slowly than the $t^{2/3}$ of matter, since radiation also loses energy to redshift.
As $a\propto t^{2/3}$ for both, because the Friedmann equation does not depend on the equation of state.
As $a\propto t^{3/2}$, faster than matter, because radiation pressure pushes space apart.
As $a\propto e^{Ht}$, since the radiation density stays constant while space expands.
s3-l041-scale-factor-solutions-matter-ra.explanation: With $\rho_r\propto a^{-4}$ the Friedmann equation $H^2\propto\rho$ gives $\dot a\propto a^{-1}$, so $a\propto t^{1/2}$; for matter $\rho\propto a^{-3}$ gives $a\propto t^{2/3}$.

s3-l041-scale-factor-solutions-matter-ra.prompt: Explain physically why a flat universe dominated by a cosmological constant expands exponentially, and why its Hubble rate stays constant.
s3-l041-scale-factor-solutions-matter-ra.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the vacuum energy density $\rho_\Lambda$ does not dilute as space expands (it has $p=-\rho c^2$); (2) then $H^2=8\pi G\rho_\Lambda/3$ is constant, so $\dot a/a=H$ gives $a\propto e^{Ht}$; (3) the negative pressure makes gravity repulsive ($\ddot a>0$), which is why dark energy accelerates the expansion today.
s3-l041-scale-factor-solutions-matter-ra.modelAnswer: A cosmological constant has constant energy density that does not dilute as space grows, so $H^2\propto\rho_\Lambda$ is constant and $\dot a/a=H$ integrates to $a\propto e^{Ht}$. Its negative pressure makes gravity repulsive, giving accelerated expansion.

s3-l042-comoving-distance-horizons-curve.prompt: The particle horizon today is about 46 billion light-years in comoving distance, though the universe is only 13.8 billion years old. How is this possible?
options: Light travelled faster than $c$ during the early universe, covering a larger distance than $ct$.
The age of the universe is underestimated; the true age must be about 46 billion years.
Distant galaxies move through space faster than $c$ relative to us, which carries them 46 Gly away.
Light has travelled since the Big Bang, but space expanded meanwhile, carrying its sources farther away.
s3-l042-comoving-distance-horizons-curve.explanation: The horizon is $d_{\rm hor} = a(t)\int c\,dt'/a(t')$, which exceeds $ct$ when $a$ grows. It marks the farthest point we could, in principle, have received signals from. It is not an edge of the universe.

s3-l042-comoving-distance-horizons-curve.prompt: What do the labels closed ($k=+1$), flat ($k=0$) and open ($k=-1$) FRW models tell us?
options: The universe's fate: closed ones always recollapse, open ones always expand, flat ones stall, whatever the cosmological constant.
The geometry of space at fixed cosmic time; with Lambda, geometry alone does not fix the fate of the expansion.
A closed universe has a boundary beyond which there is nothing, and an open universe is infinite but has an edge.
Flat means no matter content, while closed and open give the sign of the matter's net energy.
s3-l042-comoving-distance-horizons-curve.explanation: In matter-only models the spatial curvature is tied to the fate of the expansion. With $\Lambda$, a closed universe can expand forever. Observations (CMB) find $|\Omega_k|\lesssim 10^{-3}$, consistent with flat.

s3-l042-comoving-distance-horizons-curve.prompt: In a flat $\Lambda$CDM universe with $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc, $\Omega_m = 0.3$ and $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.7$, $H(z) = H_0\sqrt{0.3(1+z)^3 + 0.7}$. Evaluate the comoving distance $\chi(z) = \int_0^z c\,dz'/H(z')$ to a galaxy at $z = 1$, in Mpc. ($c = 2.998\times10^5$ km/s.)
s3-l042-comoving-distance-horizons-curve.explanation: Numerical integration gives $\chi = 3304$ Mpc (about 10.8 billion light-years). The integrand falls as $H$ grows, so the distance is less than the naive $cz/H_0 = 4283$ Mpc.

s3-l042-comoving-distance-horizons-curve.prompt: Explain what the particle horizon is, why it is not simply $c$ times the age of the universe, and how it differs from the event horizon.
s3-l042-comoving-distance-horizons-curve.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the particle horizon is the largest comoving distance from which light could have reached us since the Big Bang, $\chi=c\int dt/a$; (2) expansion carries the sources away while the light travels, so the present distance (about 46 billion light-years) exceeds $ct$ (about 13.8 billion); (3) the event horizon is the limit of what we will ever see in the future, finite in an accelerating universe, whereas the particle horizon concerns the past.
s3-l042-comoving-distance-horizons-curve.modelAnswer: The particle horizon is the farthest comoving distance whose light has reached us since the Big Bang; because space expanded while the light travelled, it is about 46 billion light-years, larger than $ct$. The event horizon instead marks the limit of what we can ever see in the future and is finite in an accelerating universe.

s3-l043-observational-cosmology-lcdm.prompt: Distant Type Ia supernovae are fainter than a matter-only decelerating universe would predict. What is the most natural interpretation?
options: The universe is decelerating even more strongly than a matter-only model predicts.
Space is positively curved, which dims every distant source by an overall factor.
The expansion accelerated recently, which requires something like a cosmological constant.
Gravity is stronger at large distances, which slows the light coming from supernovae.
s3-l043-observational-cosmology-lcdm.explanation: Luminosity distance depends on the integral $\int dz/H(z)$. A larger distance at given redshift means $H$ was lower in the past relative to a matter-only model, i.e. acceleration. Combined with the CMB (flat geometry) and BAO, this gives $\Omega_m\approx0.3$, $\Omega_\Lambda\approx0.7$.

s3-l043-observational-cosmology-lcdm.prompt: Cosmologists combine supernovae, the CMB and baryon acoustic oscillations to constrain the expansion history. In your own words, explain how each depends on $H(z)$ and why combining them is more powerful than any one alone.
s3-l043-observational-cosmology-lcdm.rubric: Full credit: (1) distances such as comoving/luminosity/angular-diameter distance are integrals of $1/H(z)$, so each probe constrains an integral of the expansion history; (2) supernovae give luminosity distance (standard candles) vs $z$, mainly sensitive to acceleration; CMB peaks and BAO provide standard rulers (angular scales) fixing curvature and matter density; (3) each probe has degeneracies in $\Omega_m$–$\Omega_\Lambda$–$H_0$ that are broken in combination (different directions in parameter space).
s3-l043-observational-cosmology-lcdm.modelAnswer: Distances are integrals of $1/H(z)$, so each probe measures some combination of the density parameters in $H^2 = H_0^2[\Omega_m(1+z)^3 + \Omega_r(1+z)^4 + \Omega_k(1+z)^2 + \Omega_\Lambda]$. Supernovae (standard candles) measure luminosity distance versus redshift and are sensitive to acceleration; the CMB peaks and BAO are standard rulers, giving angular sizes that fix the geometry and matter density. Each leaves a degeneracy in the parameter space, but the degeneracy directions differ, so the intersection pins down $\Omega_m \approx 0.3$ and $\Omega_\Lambda \approx 0.7$.

s3-l043-observational-cosmology-lcdm.prompt: The Hubble constant inferred from the CMB (assuming $\Lambda$CDM) is about 67 km/s/Mpc, while local distance-ladder measurements give about 73. What is the status of this 'H0 tension'?
options: It was resolved by a calibration error in the CMB, so the two values now agree to 1%.
It proves that general relativity fails on cosmological scales and must be replaced.
It is statistical noise, since the two methods agree within their quoted uncertainties.
A statistically significant discrepancy whose cause, new physics or unrecognized systematics, is still debated.
s3-l043-observational-cosmology-lcdm.explanation: The two routes disagree by roughly 8%, far outside their stated errors, and no consensus exists on whether it signals missing physics in $\Lambda$CDM or an unaccounted systematic in one of the methods.

s3-l043-observational-cosmology-lcdm.prompt: The critical density today is $\rho_c=3H_0^2/(8\pi G)$. For $H_0=70$ km/s/Mpc (1 Mpc $=3.086\times10^{22}$ m, $G=6.674\times10^{-11}$ SI), find $\rho_c$ in units of $10^{-27}$ kg/m$^3$.
s3-l043-observational-cosmology-lcdm.explanation: $\rho_c=3H_0^2/8\pi G\approx9.2\times10^{-27}$ kg/m$^3$, about five hydrogen atoms per cubic metre.
